usage: Do you have a power bank?
asking to borrow one; just the bare noun + 있어요 carries the whole request
충전하다 = charge; here the bank is the thing being charged, not your phone
I'll lend you my power bank
빌려주다 = lend; -ㄹ게요 makes it a friendly offer
대용량 = large-capacity, the word you scan for when shopping
examples: 보조배터리 있어요?
Do you have a power bank?
simplest form: the noun alone + 있다 is a complete, natural question
폰이 꺼져서 보조배터리를 챙겼어요.
My phone died so I packed a power bank.
챙기다 = grab/pack to bring along; note the object particle 를 on 보조배터리
혹시 보조배터리 잠깐만 빌릴 수 있을까요?
Could I maybe borrow your power bank for just a sec?
혹시 + -ㄹ 수 있을까요 = the soft, polite way to ask a stranger a favor
nuance: 보조배터리 is the everyday word for a portable power bank, and it is built transparently from 보조(補助, 'auxiliary/supplementary') + 배터리, literally 'auxiliary battery' — so the name itself tells you it is the spare, not your phone's built-in cell. Almost every Korean in their 20s–30s carries one, so it surfaces constantly in casual talk; unlike many long loan-compounds it is rarely clipped — people just say the full 보조배터리, so as a learner say it in full and you'll be understood everywhere. The English loanword 파워뱅크 (power bank) exists but many people will not recognize it, so default to 보조배터리. The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: do not assume the English term transfers, and watch the particle — 보조배터리를 충전하다 means charging the bank itself, whereas 보조배터리로 충전하다 (with 로, 'by means of') means using it to charge something else.

usage: 깨지다 = break/shatter; the go-to verb for reporting phone damage
수리(修理) = repair; what you ask for at the counter
교체(交替) = swap/replace; pricier than a 수리
a crack line forms on the screen
금이 가다 = a hairline crack appears, lighter than fully 깨지다
examples: 액정이 깨졌어요.
The screen cracked.
the core sentence you say first at a repair shop
폰을 떨어뜨려서 액정이 다 깨졌어요.
I dropped my phone and the screen is totally shattered.
떨어뜨리다 = drop something; 다 = completely
액정 교체하는 데 얼마나 들어요?
How much does it cost to replace the screen?
-는 데 (드는 비용) = the cost it takes to do something
nuance: 액정 is Sino-Korean 液晶(液 'liquid' + 晶 'crystal') — literally 'liquid crystal', i.e. LCD — and in daily speech it means the physical glass display panel of a phone. The sharp contrast a learner must keep is 액정 vs 화면(畫面, 'screen/display'): 화면 leans toward what is shown ON the screen (the picture, the UI, 'the screen went black'), while 액정 is the tangible panel that gets dropped, cracked, repaired and replaced. So damage talk almost always uses 액정 (액정이 깨졌어요), and content talk uses 화면 (화면이 안 보여요). It collocates tightly with 깨지다 / 금이 가다 / 수리 / 교체. Pronunciation pitfall: 액정 is said [액쩡] with a tensed 쩡, and do not confuse the written word with 액체(liquid) — they share 액 but are unrelated in meaning.

Pronouncing it [액정] flat instead of the tensed [액쩡].
Confusing 액정 with 액체 (liquid) — same first syllable, totally different word.

usage: 기간(期間) = span of time; e.g. 2년 약정 기간
끝나다 = end; the moment you're free to switch carriers
the typical lock-in length when you buy a subsidized phone
위약금(違約金) = breach-of-contract fee charged for leaving early
examples: 저는 2년 약정이에요.
I'm on a 2-year contract.
simple noun-이에요 statement of your status
2년 약정으로 폰을 싸게 샀어요.
I got the phone cheap on a 2-year contract.
-으로 = by means of/under (the contract); the carrier subsidizes the price
약정이 아직 안 끝나서 위약금이 나와요.
My contract isn't over yet, so there's a penalty.
위약금이 나오다 = a penalty gets charged; -아서 links cause to result
nuance: 약정 is Sino-Korean 約定(約 'promise/bind' + 定 'fix/settle') — a 'fixed, bound agreement' — and in everyday life it almost always means the carrier lock-in period you accept in exchange for a discounted phone. The boundaries learners blur: 계약(契約) is the broad word for a contract you sign (a lease, a job), while 약정 specifically names the telecom/finance lock-in term; and 약속(約束, a personal promise between people) shares the 約 character but is a completely different register — you keep a 약속 with a friend, you are bound by a 약정 with a company. It collocates with 기간, 끝나다, 남다(be left), 위약금. The pitfall: an English speaker may reach for 계약 or even 약속 to say 'my phone contract', but Koreans say 약정 — '약정이 남았어요?' (Is your contract still running?) is the natural phrasing.

Saying '약정이 끝냈어요' (transitive 끝내다, 'I ended it') when you mean it ended on its own — use the intransitive '약정이 끝났어요'.

usage: 바꾸다 = change; what you do when your 약정 ends
매장 = retail store; where you sign up or 개통
discount points and coupons tied to your provider
알뜰 = thrifty; cheaper providers riding the big networks
examples: 어느 통신사 써요?
Which carrier do you use?
어느 = which (among a known set); a standard getting-to-know-you question
통신사 멤버십으로 영화표를 할인받았어요.
I got a movie-ticket discount with my carrier membership.
-으로 = by means of; 할인받다 = receive a discount
외국인도 통신사 매장에서 바로 개통할 수 있어요.
Foreigners can activate a line right at a carrier store too.
개통하다 = activate phone service; 도 = even/too
nuance: 통신사 is Sino-Korean 通信社 — 通信(通 'communicate' + 信 'message/signal') + 社('company') = 'communications company', i.e. a mobile/telecom provider like SKT, KT, or LG U+, plus the cheaper 알뜰폰 MVNOs. The contrast to hold: 통신사 = the network/service provider you pay monthly, whereas 제조사(製造社, the maker — 삼성, 애플) is who built the handset, and 폰 회사 is ambiguous between the two. Because 요금제(plans), 약정, and 멤버십 differ by provider, '어느 통신사 써요?' is a genuinely frequent question. Two pitfalls: 통신사 can also mean a 'news agency' (as in 연합뉴스 같은 통신사) in formal contexts, but in daily phone talk it is the carrier; and English speakers often say '폰 회사' thinking 'phone company', which Koreans hear as the manufacturer — say 통신사 for the carrier.

usage: -하다 turns the loanword noun into a verb
the phrasing a notification uses: 새 업데이트가 있어요
-중(中) = in the middle of; shown on the loading screen
examples: 업데이트했어요.
I updated it.
the loanword + 했어요 is already a full natural sentence
앱이 자꾸 꺼져서 업데이트를 했어요.
The app kept crashing so I updated it.
꺼지다 = (app) shuts off/crashes; 자꾸 = repeatedly
지금 업데이트 중이라 좀 기다려야 해요.
It's updating right now, so I have to wait a bit.
-(이)라 = because it is (a casual reason link from -중)
nuance: 업데이트 is the English loanword used for refreshing software, an app, or your phone's OS to the latest version. The contrast Koreans actually feel is 업데이트 vs 업그레이드: 업데이트 means getting the newest version/patches (bug fixes, new features), while 업그레이드(upgrade) implies moving up a tier or spec — better hardware, a higher plan, a paid premium level. So a routine version refresh is 업데이트, and 'I upgraded to a better phone/plan' is 업그레이드. It collocates with 하다, 있다, 자동, 중. Two pitfalls for English speakers: do not use 업데이트 and 업그레이드 interchangeably the way casual English sometimes does — Korean keeps them distinct; and because it is a noun, you must attach -하다 to make the verb (업데이트해요), not leave it bare as if it were already a verb.

Leaving the noun bare as a verb — say '업데이트해요/업데이트했어요', attaching -하다, not just '업데이트요'.
Forgetting the object particle when needed — '업데이트를 했어요' is cleaner than dropping it in writing, though speech often omits it.

usage: 부족하다(不足) = be insufficient; the #1 phrase you'll hear
저장(貯藏) = storage/saving; specifies it's storage, not data/volume
꽉 차다 = be packed full; 꽉 intensifies
examples: 용량이 부족해요.
I'm low on storage.
the everyday complaint in its simplest form
사진이 너무 많아서 용량이 부족해요.
I have too many photos, so I'm low on storage.
-아서 = so/because; the classic cause of full storage
용량이 꽉 차서 앱이 설치가 안 돼요.
Storage is full so the app won't install.
설치(設置) = installation; 안 되다 = won't work
nuance: 용량 is Sino-Korean 容量(容 'hold/contain' + 量 'amount/quantity') = 'the amount that can be held', so it covers a phone's storage, a file's size, a data amount, and even the volume a bowl or container can hold. In the phone context it almost always means 저장 용량 (storage), and 용량이 부족하다 / 꽉 차다 are the phrases you meet constantly. Watch two boundaries: a mobile data allowance is sometimes called 용량 informally, but it is usually said as 데이터 or in GB, so keep 용량 for storage to be clear; and crucially, 용량 is NOT 'volume' in the loudness sense — sound level is 볼륨(volume) or 소리. The English-speaker trap is hearing 'capacity/volume' and reaching for 볼륨, or expecting 용량 to mean only data — anchor it to physical/storage capacity (256기가 용량 = 256GB of storage).

usage: 본인(本人) = the person themselves; proving you are you
the one-time SMS code you type in
-하다 makes the noun a verb; complete the verification
verifying your identity via your mobile number
examples: 인증번호가 왔어요.
The verification code arrived.
오다 = come/arrive; the code 'comes' to you by text
가입하려면 본인 인증을 먼저 해야 해요.
To sign up you have to verify your identity first.
-려면 = if you intend to; 가입하다 = sign up
외국인등록증으로도 인증이 되나요?
Can I verify with my alien registration card too?
-으로 = using; 인증이 되다 = verification goes through; a key resident question
nuance: 인증 is Sino-Korean 認證(認 'recognize/acknowledge' + 證 'proof/certify') = 'certified recognition', i.e. authentication or verification. In Korea nearly every sign-up, payment, and booking requires 본인 인증, so it is essential vocabulary for foreign residents — typically you receive an 인증번호 by text and enter it, and without it you often cannot use the service at all. The look-alike to separate is 인정(認定, acknowledgement/recognition, as in '인정받다' = to be recognized/credited): 인증 and 인정 share the 認 character and look similar but mean different things. Also keep 인증번호(a one-time verification code) distinct from 비밀번호(your password) — English speakers often call the SMS code a 'password', but Koreans call the disposable code an 인증번호 and the reusable secret a 비밀번호.

usage: -하다 verb; save a copy of your data
받다 here = obtain/create a copy onto storage
자동(自動) = automatic; runs by itself to the cloud
안 되다 = fail/not work; common troubleshooting phrase
examples: 백업했어요?
Did you back it up?
loanword + 했어요 question; the first thing asked before a phone swap
폰 바꾸기 전에 백업부터 해 두세요.
Back things up before you switch phones.
-기 전에 = before doing; -아/어 두다 = do in advance and leave it done
백업을 안 해서 연락처가 다 날아갔어요.
I didn't back up, so I lost all my contacts.
날아가다 = (data) gets wiped/lost; -아서 links cause to result
nuance: 백업 is the English loanword 'backup' used specifically for copying data — phone backups, cloud backups, contacts and photos. Because Koreans change and reset phones often, 백업 is thoroughly everyday vocabulary; the verb is both 백업하다 and 백업받다, and whether your 자동 백업 to the cloud is on is a frequent topic. The key contrast is 백업 vs 저장(貯藏, 'save'): 저장하다 is saving a file in place (saving a document), while 백업하다 means making a separate spare copy for safety — so they are not interchangeable. The English-speaker pitfall is the other English sense of 'backup' (a substitute person, reinforcements, 'I'll back you up'): that meaning does NOT carry into Korean 백업, which in daily life is almost exclusively the data sense — for human backup you'd use words like 지원/대체 instead.

usage: 들어가다 = enter; 에 marks the place you go into
알림 = notification; the submenu for alerts
바꾸다 = change; 을 marks the setting as the object
초기(初期) = initial/early stage; first-time configuration
examples: 설정에 들어가세요.
Go into Settings.
-(으)세요 polite command; 에 = into (the menu)
언어 설정을 영어로 바꿀 수 있어요?
Can I change the language setting to English?
-로 = into/to (the result); a very useful new-resident question
설정이 어디 있는지 못 찾겠어요.
I can't find where the settings are.
-는지 = the embedded question 'where'; 못 찾겠다 = can't manage to find
nuance: 설정 is Sino-Korean 設定(設 'set up/establish' + 定 'fix/determine') = 'to set and fix', the standard word for the configuration menu on a phone or app — it is exactly what sits where English shows 'Settings'. Just knowing 설정에 들어가다(go in) and 설정을 바꾸다(change a setting) lets you follow a shop clerk's or friend's instructions easily. The contrast to note: 설정 is the configurable preference, while 설치(設置, installation) is putting an app on, and 설명(說明, explanation) merely looks similar in writing. Mind two things as an English speaker: you can say 세팅(setting) and be understood, but the on-screen menu is almost always labeled 설정, so learn that form; and do not visually confuse 설정(settings) with 설명(explanation) — they share 설 but differ.

usage: 기종 = device type/model; pairs with 뭐예요 to ask which one
같은 = same; e.g. sharing a charger because 같은 기종
구형(舊型) = old-type; opposite of 신형 newer model
변경(變更) = change; switching to a different handset
examples: 폰 기종이 뭐예요?
What phone model is it?
noun + 이/가 뭐예요 = the basic 'what is X?' question
이 앱은 구형 기종에서는 안 돌아가요.
This app doesn't run on older models.
-에서는 = on/in (contrast); 돌아가다 = (software) runs
같은 기종이라 충전기를 같이 써요.
It's the same model, so we share a charger.
-(이)라 = because it is; 같이 = together
nuance: 기종 is Sino-Korean 機種(機 'machine/device' + 種 'kind/type') = 'kind of machine', i.e. the specific model of a device — phones above all, but also cameras, cars, and appliances. When buying a case or film, getting a repair, or doing a used-resale, '기종이 뭐예요?' is nearly mandatory because accessories must match the exact model. The boundary worth noting: 기종 is the model/type of a device, 모델 is the English loanword that also works and is common in ads, while 기계(機械) is 'machine' in the general sense — so 기종 is more precise than 기계 when you mean which model. The English-speaker pitfalls: 'model' translates fine as 모델, but 기종 often sounds more natural in spoken Korean (especially for phones); and do not let the sound drift toward 기분(mood/feeling) — it is [기종], a different word entirely.

usage: 붙이다 = stick/apply on; the verb for putting film on
the film lifts up at the edges
들뜨다 = peel/lift away from the surface
강화유리(強化琉璃) = tempered glass; the sturdier kind
교체(交替) = swap/replace; redoing a worn protector
examples: 필름 붙였어요?
Did you put a screen protector on?
in real life it's clipped to just '필름'; 붙이다 = apply
새 폰 사서 화면보호필름부터 붙였어요.
I bought a new phone and put a protector on first.
-부터 = starting with; the customary first step
필름이 깨져서 액정은 멀쩡해요.
The film cracked, so the screen itself is fine.
멀쩡하다 = perfectly intact; the film did its job
nuance: 화면보호필름 is a transparent compound — 화면(畫面, 'screen/display') + 보호(保護, 'protect') + 필름(film, loanword) = 'screen-protecting film' — but in real speech almost everyone clips it to just 필름. Putting one on is a near-universal first step with a new phone, and shop staff routinely offer '필름도 같이 붙여 드릴까요?' (Shall I put the film on too?). The contrast to register: 화면보호필름/필름 is the thin protective sheet on the glass, distinct from 케이스(the case around the body) and from the 액정 (the actual display panel underneath) — the film sacrifices itself so the 액정 survives. Two English-speaker pitfalls: do not picture photographic film or movie 'film' — in the phone context 필름 is the protector sheet; and keep 붙이다(stick/apply) separate from the similar-sounding 부치다(to mail something, or to pan-fry) — '필름 붙여 주세요' uses 붙이다.

usage: the prototypical subject; describes a change for the worse
갑자기 = all of a sudden; an abrupt drop
점점 = little by little; a creeping decline
speed dropping over time or under load
examples: 폰이 느려졌어요.
My phone has gotten slow.
past -어졌어요 states the result: it became slow
용량이 꽉 차면 폰이 느려져요.
When storage is full, the phone slows down.
-(으)면 = whenever/if; a cause-and-effect statement
저녁만 되면 와이파이가 느려져요.
The wifi gets slow every evening.
-만 되면 = the moment it just becomes (every time); recurring trigger
nuance: 느려지다 is the inchoative pair of the adjective 느리다(be slow): 느리다 + the -어지다 'become' ending = 'to get/grow slow', so the form itself encodes change. The required conjugation logic shows on the 요-form: 느리다 → stem 느리- + 어지다, and because the stem already ends in 이, it contracts to 느려지다 → 느려져요 (present), 느려졌어요 (past) — the 어 of -어지다 fuses with 이 to give 려. The sharp contrast is exactly 느리다 vs 느려지다: 느리다 describes a steady state ('this phone IS slow'), while 느려지다 describes the transition ('it GOT slow / is getting slower'), which is why complaints about a phone degrading use 느려지다 with 점점/갑자기. The English-speaker pitfall: English 'slow' is one word, so learners say 느려요 for everything, but to express that something has worsened over time you need 느려졌어요; also do not confuse it with the look-alike 늘어지다(stretch/drag out, go limp).

mistakes: Using the state adjective 느리다 (느려요) when you mean it WORSENED — for a change over time, say '느려졌어요' (느려지다).
